oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Fifteenth of Av is the Yom Tov of the future redemption, felt in the heart of Klal Yisrael, the day Yirmiyahu of Tisha B'Av turns back into Shlomo HaMelech.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah at the end of Taanis and asks why it ends with Shlomo HaMelech, why the daughters danced in the vineyards, and why the Gemara needs six reasons for a day greater than Pesach. He asks why the Shulchan Aruch's calendar sign omits the seventh day of Pesach, and answers that it determines the Fifteenth of Av, a Yom Tov for a redemption that has not yet come. The six reasons are the reflected light of that future joy, the dance Hashem will make for the tzaddikim. Women grasp the redemption with feeling, so the daughters dance in the vineyards. He then sets Tisha B'Av against Shemini Atzeres and Yirmiyahu against Shlomo, quoting the Chasam Sofer that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo. On the Fifteenth of Av one takes off Yirmiyahu's garments, adds in Torah, builds one's own Mikdash and rises from the grave of Tisha B'Av.

en: The seventh day of Pesach, the 'Shabbos' of Pesach, determines the weekday of the Fifteenth of Av, which is left out of the calendar sign because it celebrates a redemption still to come.
The Gemara's six reasons are true, but they are the reflected light of the real, seventh reason: the future dance Hashem will make for the tzaddikim.
Belief in the redemption comes from the heart and feeling, which is why the daughters, not the sons, go out to dance in the vineyards, the place of wine.
Tisha B'Av corresponds to Shemini Atzeres, and Yirmiyahu, the prophet of the destruction, is a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, whose day is Shemini Atzeres.
Every Jew has in him a Yirmiyahu and a Shlomo; on the Fifteenth of Av he should add in Torah, take on new resolutions and build his own Mikdash.
Shlomo conquered the whole world without war, through peace and Torah, and so he is the soul of the days of Moshiach.

title.en: The Mishnah's Fifteenth of Av and its puzzles

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Mishnah at the end of Taanis about the daughters going out in borrowed white garments, ending with 'tze'enah ur'enah' and Shlomo HaMelech. He asks what Shlomo has to do with the Fifteenth of Av, why the Baraisa adds that they danced in the vineyards, and why the passuk speaks of daughters going to see the king.

title.en: Six reasons for one Yom Tov

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that asks what happened on the Fifteenth of Av and gives six reasons. He argues, with a mashal of a boy late to cheder, that many reasons weaken each other, and that reasons like the tribes intermarrying or the wood for the altar cannot explain a day greater than Pesach, Shavuos and Sukkos.

title.en: Why the seventh day of Pesach is missing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the sign of the Shulchan Aruch by which each day of Pesach fixes the weekday of a later festival, since Pesach is the head of all festivals. He asks why the seventh day, the highest day of Pesach, is left out, when it would fix the Fifteenth of Av, both falling on Friday this year.

title.en: A Yom Tov for what is yet to come

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that the Fifteenth of Av follows Tisha B'Av, ending its seven days of mourning, and is fixed by the seventh day of Pesach, its Shabbos. The sign lists festivals for events that already happened, while the Fifteenth of Av celebrates the coming redemption, Nachamu, when a Jew should engrave in himself emunah in Moshiach.

title.en: The hidden seventh reason

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every holy event casts its light before it happens, as Avraham ate matzos and wonders happened on Pesach night before the Exodus. The Gemara's six reasons are that reflected light; the seventh is Rabbi Elazar's teaching that Hashem will make a dance for the tzaddikim, which the daughters' dancing hints at.

title.en: Feeling and intellect: why the daughters dance

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gevuros Hashem that the matzos correspond to the Avos and the mind, the four cups of wine to the Imahos and feeling. He shows from Bnos Tzelofchad and from Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen that belief in the redemption is felt in the heart, and so the daughters dance in the vineyards, the place of wine.

title.en: Nachamu, Hashem comforts with the prophet

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Pesikta that the people would accept comfort only from Hashem Himself, so Hashem goes with Yeshayahu into every shul on the seven Shabbosos of consolation. The seventh haftarah, 'sos asis', corresponds to the seventh of Pesach and speaks of chassan and kallah; the borrowed garments, as the Bnei Yissaschar says, are borrowed from the future.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres, the day of Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach sets Shemini Atzeres, the most joyful day, against Tisha B'Av, the saddest. He brings the Chasam Sofer that all festivals prepare for Shemini Atzeres, the haftarah of Shlomo completing the Beis HaMikdash, the Midrash that Shlomo was the fifteenth generation like the full moon, and Rebbe Reb Bunim that Shemini Atzeres is Shlomo's day.

title.en: Yirmiyahu, the prophet of Tisha B'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yirmiyahu was born on Tisha B'Av, so 'cursed is the day I was born' states a fact. With the Midrash's mashal of a kohen who must disgrace his own mother, he describes Yirmiyahu's bitter lot, and contrasts it with Shlomo's era of peace, 'each man under his vine', against Yirmiyahu's 'no grapes on the vine'.

title.en: Yirmiyahu, a gilgul of Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo: because Shlomo slept late on the day the Beis HaMikdash was dedicated, he had to return as Yirmiyahu and see its destruction. Hidden in Tisha B'Av lies the birth of Moshiach, and Yirmiyahu will yet bless the day he was born.

title.en: Eichah against Shir HaShirim

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes twenty-two days in each of bein hametzarim and Rosh Hashanah to Shemini Atzeres, so Tisha B'Av corresponds to Shemini Atzeres. He pictures Yirmiyahu finishing Eichah and remembering that as Shlomo he wrote Shir HaShirim, and explains why, when Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos as this year, one eats 'like the meal of Shlomo in his time'.

title.en: The black background, from Yirmiyahu to Yeshayahu

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a Lubavitch teaching that the three weeks through Shemini Atzeres are like a colorful embroidery on a black background, and adds that the reading of Tisha B'Av already hints at 'atah hor'eisa' of the hakafos. From the Fifteenth of Av one exchanges Yirmiyahu's garments for Shlomo's crown, and Yeshayahu, the prophet of consolation, is the prophet of Shemini Atzeres.

title.en: Shlomo conquered the world with peace

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shlomo ruled the whole world without ever going to war, an 'ish menuchah', and is the soul of Moshiach. He tells that at the judgment of the two women no sword could be found among his soldiers, and one had to be brought from a museum, because Shlomo conquered with Torah.

title.en: Putting on Shlomo's garments; build your own Mikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on the Fifteenth of Av, after the seven days of mourning, Yirmiyahu turns into Shlomo, and the Mishnah's 'day of his wedding' and 'day of his heart's joy' mean taking on new Torah and building the Mikdash. Every Jew has a Yirmiyahu and a Shlomo, and he should build his own Mikdash, since what a Jew does Hashem does too; this is done through good middos.

title.en: Jews who are festivals

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Tisha B'Av is called a mo'ed and that Jews themselves are mo'adim: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is Shabbos, a talmid chacham is Shabbos who gives to the weekday Jews, and there are Jews who are Yom Tov, Chol HaMoed, Pesach, Shavuos or Sukkos. He tells, as Tosafos brings, how the generation of the desert lay down in graves every Tisha B'Av until the fortieth year.

title.en: Reb Tisha B'Av, rise from the grave

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a gifted young man, 'Reb Tisha B'Av', who wastes his powers and lies in a grave. On the Fifteenth of Av, the start of preparation for the Days of Awe, one makes a cheshbon hanefesh, adds in Torah, leaves the grave and looks at the Torah, the 'eishes chayil'. He ends with a brachah for new luchos and to see Yirmiyahu in the garments of Shlomo.

catalogTitle: זמן לשאוב יראת שמים בעד הכנה לר"ה' זמן של שידוכים' ז' ימים אחר היו"ט הגדול של ט' באב לעתיד.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Chamishah Asar b'Av as the start of the season of yiras shamayim and teshuvah leading to Yom Kippur, a day of shidduchim between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and the yom tov of the hidden good in the churban: that the avodah of Jews in galus is more precious to Hashem than ever, which is why one adds in Torah from that day.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with parshas Eikev and its haftarah as the week of yiras Hashem within the seven weeks of comfort, and with the tradition that the days of teshuvah begin on the fifteenth of Av. Using the Mishnah about the girls of Yerushalayim, he describes the day as a shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael whose tenaim are the passuk of fearing and loving Hashem. A story about a man in Biala who chose his purchase right after Yom Kippur shows that a person's choice is good when he is free of sin, and the Mashgiach explains that Yom Kippur's power already begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av. He then contrasts holy fear, which comes from wholeness, with fear born of lack. In the second part he explains, through the Pesikta on 'Sing, O barren one' and the words of the Arizal, the Chiddushei HaRim and the Chasam Sofer, that avodah in galus is more precious than in the times of the Beis Hamikdash. Chamishah Asar b'Av is the day to rejoice in this and to add in Torah.

en: Chamishah Asar b'Av is a time to draw yiras shamayim, falling in the week of parshas Eikev, the week of fear of Hashem among the seven weeks of comfort, and it opens the days of teshuvah.
The day of shidduchim is a shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and its tenaim are the passuk 'What does Hashem ask of you, but to fear Hashem… and to love Him'.
Yom Kippur makes a person free of sin, so his choice is good, and since the process of Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av, that day too is a time when a Jew's choice is at its best.

Since the churban, the avodah of Jews in galus is more precious to Hashem than the avodah of the great tzaddikim of the Beis Hamikdash era, as the Pesikta teaches on 'the children of the desolate are more than the children of the married one'.

On Chamishah Asar b'Av, rising from the mourning of Tisha b'Av, one rejoices that our avodah is precious, makes a reckoning that the opportunity may end when Moshiach comes, and adds in Torah, tefillah and Yiddishkeit.

title.en: The week of yiras Hashem and the start of teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach presents parshas Eikev and its haftarah as the week of yiras Hashem among the seven weeks of comfort, recalls that Rebbe Reb Bunim learned Sefer Devarim as his mussar, and brings the tradition that the days of teshuvah begin on Chamishah Asar b'Av. He reads the Mishnah about the girls of Yerushalayim and calls the day a time to draw yiras shamayim.

title.en: A shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the day of shidduchim as the time when Hashem chooses Klal Yisrael, who in galus say 'do not look at me for I am dark', and says the tenaim of this shidduch are the passuk of fearing and loving Hashem. He ends with a story of a Chernobyler tzaddik.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: Choosing right after Yom Kippur: the man from Biala

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that a person's match is announced from heaven but one must merit to receive it, and that matches were once chosen around Yom Kippur. He tells of a man in Biala who picked a sealed box right after Yom Kippur and always had the finest in town, explaining that free of sin, his choice was sure to be good.

title.en: Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yom Kippur is a day when a Jew's nature and choice incline to good, and that the avodah of teshuvah which ends on Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av, so the end is already in the beginning. On this day a Jew's choice is at its best, and he applies 'u'vacharta ba'chaim' and the call to the young man to lift his eyes: to choose a path of Torah.

title.en: Av, Yerushalayim and a fear born of wholeness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Av and Yerushalayim, joy for the whole world in time and in place, became mourning with the churban, and that from Chamishah Asar b'Av the rebuilding begins. Yerushalayim is 'yirah shleimah': holy fear comes from wholeness, unlike ordinary fear, which comes from what a person lacks, as one fears a lion.

title.en: Why avodah in galus is so precious

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Gemara's reasons for Chamishah Asar b'Av hide a deep inner meaning, and that some of it may now be said as Moshiach approaches. Relying on the Chiddushei HaRim and the Pesikta on 'Sing, O barren one', and on the Arizal's words to R' Chaim Vital, he explains that the avodah of Jews in galus is more precious to Hashem than that of the giants of the Beis Hamikdash era.

title.en: The two sides of Tisha b'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chiddushei HaRim, who rose from shivah for his brother on Chamishah Asar b'Av, and asks why the end of mourning should be a yom tov. He answers that Tisha b'Av holds two opposite things: the churban and hester panim, which grow each year, and the gain that our avodah is now more precious; but on Tisha b'Av one cannot rejoice in that gain, since the honor of Hashem requires the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Rejoicing and making a reckoning

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that for ourselves galus is better, since in the days of Moshiach there is no difficulty in serving Hashem, and we pray for the Beis Hamikdash only for the honor of Heaven. Therefore, once the mourning ends, Chamishah Asar b'Av was set as a day to rejoice that we are precious to Hashem and to make a reckoning to grab more Torah and mitzvos now.

title.en: Adding in Torah from Chamishah Asar b'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara's call to add in learning from Chamishah Asar b'Av: not because the nights grow longer, but because each year's new hester panim makes our avodah more precious, and Moshiach may come at any moment. One must always pray for the Beis Hamikdash, yet may make this reckoning and add in Torah, tefillah and every part of Yiddishkeit.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the dor hamidbar knew on Tu b'Av that the decree had ended because only then could they sense the moon, the middas malchus and yiras shamayim, which had been hidden since the sin of the meraglim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara's reason for the yom tov of Tu b'Av: every Tisha b'Av in the desert part of the generation died in graves they dug, and in the fortieth year they kept lying down night after night until the full moon of the fifteenth told them the decree was over. He asks how they could have doubted the date on the fourteenth, when the moon is almost full. He tells how the Radziner Rebbe brought his techeiles to the Sfas Emes, who said he did not smell techeiles. Through the Ramchal's question on the berachah of Yotzer and the Divrei Yoel on Rabbeinu Tam, he develops an upper and a lower sun and moon. The moon is malchus and yiras shamayim, which is the sense of smell; after the meraglim it was hidden, and on Tu b'Av, the start of the awakening toward Rosh Hashanah, they sensed it again.

en: In the fortieth year the dor hamidbar lay down in their graves night after night, and only the full moon of the fifteenth of Av showed them the decree was over, so they made a yom tov.
There is an upper sun and moon and a lower sun and moon; the visible sun's power to sustain the world comes down from the upper sun each dawn through the tzimtzumim.
The moon is middas malchus, which is yiras shamayim, and yiras shamayim is the sense of smell; therefore the moon is called yareach, from rei'ach, smell.
Since the sin of the meraglim there was hester panim: the physical moon was there, but the moon one can 'smell' was hidden.
Tu b'Av is when the awakening toward Rosh Hashanah begins, and on it the dor hamidbar sensed the moon, middas malchus, revealed again.

title.en: Why Tu b'Av is a yom tov

summary.en: After opening singing, the Mashgiach brings the Gemara's reason for Tu b'Av: each Tisha b'Av in the desert part of the generation died in graves they had dug, and in the fortieth year they lay down night after night until the full moon of the fifteenth showed them the decree was over.

title.en: A question, and the Radziner's techeiles

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how they could have thought they miscounted on the fourteenth, when the moon is nearly full. He then tells how the Radziner Rebbe found the chilazon, made techeiles and argued for it, and how the Sfas Emes held it to his nose and said he did not smell techeiles.

title.en: The upper sun and the lower sun

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramchal's question on the berachah of Yotzer, which speaks of opening the gates of the east each day, and his answer that the influence of an upper sun comes down each dawn into the visible sun. He adds the Divrei Yoel, who answers the Baal HaTanya's objection to Rabbeinu Tam's 72 minutes with the upper sun.

title.en: The moon, malchus and the sense of smell

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the moon is malchus and yiras shamayim, which is smell, so the Sfas Emes meant the techeiles lacked yiras shamayim, as there will be no techeiles until Moshiach. The moon is hidden on Rosh Hashanah until Jews crown Hashem with the shofar, and after the meraglim the 'smelled' moon was hidden altogether.

title.en: Sensing the moon on Tu b'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers his question: they thought a merit was holding off the decree day after day, as with the sotah, until on Tu b'Av they sensed the moon and malchus. Tu b'Av is when the awakening toward Rosh Hashanah and teshuvah begins, and it brings lights of geulah.

catalogTitle: המן- The Architect of his Own Demise

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that in the Megillah, where Hashem hides His face, Haman himself prepared every step of his own downfall, and that Amalek's attack on 'the end' fails because the Jewish people have no end.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the twelve months, which correspond to the twelve tribes arranged in four camps. Nisan, the month of Yehuda and of the miracles of Egypt, comes first; the months descend until Adar, the last, whose Megillah has no open miracle at all. This is hester panim: Hashem hides, yet controls everything, and every small story in the Megillah is a wheel in one mechanism. The Mashgiach reads Chazal's identification of Memuchan with Haman as a signal to watch Haman, who unknowingly prepared Esther's rise, Mordechai's honor, his house and his own gallows. Adar means a cloak, and Dan is the last and most removed tribe, yet his son Chushim killed Esav. Amalek attacks those at the end, outside the camp, as Haman rejoiced when the lot fell on Adar; but the Jewish people have no end, and Purim protects those at the end.

en: The months descend from Nisan, named for its miracles, to Adar, whose Megillah contains no open miracle at all.
The message of the Megillah is that even when no miracles are seen, Hashem is hidden but controls everything.
Haman prepared every element of his own downfall: Vashti's removal, Mordechai's honor, his house and the gallows.
Dan, the last tribe, is the most removed from holiness and always gets into trouble, yet he remains connected to the Shem Havayah.
Amalek attacks those at the end, outside the camp, and Haman likewise hoped to prevail in Adar, the month of the end.
The Jewish people have no end: Amalek has an end, but when the Jews finish they begin again.

title.en: Twelve months, twelve tribes, and Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach matches the twelve months to the twelve tribes in their four camps, from Nisan and Yehuda to Adar at the end. He notes that Amalek has no future, and that the months descend from Nisan's miracles to Adar's Megillah, where no open miracle appears.

title.en: Hidden face: Haman prepares everything

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's source for Esther in the Torah, hester panim, and explains that every small story in the Megillah is a wheel in one mechanism. From Chazal's identification of Memuchan with Haman he shows that Haman prepared Vashti's removal, Mordechai's greatness and his own gallows.

title.en: Only Haman knew how to do it

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls it a mockery of avodah zarah that it prepares its own demise. Mordechai, a tzaddik with rachmanus and no taste for honor, could not have devised the cruel gallows, the royal honor or the mansion; Haman did all three, unknowingly for Mordechai.

title.en: Adar the cloak; Dan and Chushim

summary.en: Returning to the months, the Mashgiach explains that Adar means a cloak, as with Esav's mantle of hair: the miracles are covered. Dan, the last and most removed tribe, still bears a permutation of the Shem Havayah, and it was Dan's son Chushim, deaf and mute, who killed Esav at Yaakov's burial.

title.en: The last generation: hester panim today

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the generation before Moshiach a generation of Chushim and of great hester panim. He recalls that in his youth there were universally accepted leaders, the last being the Chazon Ish, while today great men are accepted only by their own factions.

title.en: Amalek attacks the end; Adar Sheini

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that those of Dan expelled from the camp were outside the Clouds of Glory, so Amalek could strike the stragglers. Haman, like Amalek, rejoiced when the lot fell on Adar, the month of the end, and a leap year's Adar Sheini, likened to the last eight pesukim of the Torah, seemed even more outside the camp. His mistake: these too belong to the camp.

title.en: No end for Yidden; Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the Jews have no end: when they finish the Torah they begin Bereishis again, and Purim protects those at the end of the camp. He then speaks of the special holiness of Shushan Purim, kept today only in Yerushalayim, and of his plan to be there.
