the sigh of a simple Jew

title.en: The hardest end of the Egyptian exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he will repeat well-known things that need constant reminding, as the Mesilas Yesharim says. Following Reb Elchonon Wasserman he presents the exile in Egypt as a model of today's exile, whose final stage, just as Moshe announced the redemption, was the hardest, culminating in Pharaoh's 'tichbad ha'avodah'.

title.en: Pharaoh's aim: no time to think

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the Jews gathered on Shabbos to read scrolls handed down from Yaakov and Yosef promising redemption, and Pharaoh took even that day away. With the Mesilas Yesharim he explains that the tactic is to leave no moment of calm, and says today too there is a klipah of 'tichbad ha'avodah' that leaves no time for yishuv hadaas.

title.en: A house of slaves and the precious sigh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'mibeis avadim' as Egypt's culture of work without thought, and calls America in particular such a house. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching, via the Magen Avraham, that Pharaoh feared even the sigh of a simple, worn-out Jew who runs to daven Minchah, and the story of the Ba'al HaTanya asking his jailer 'ayeka', where are you in the world.

title.en: Forced labor then, chosen burden now

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the poverty of Jews in Europe, who worked sixteen hours a day for black bread, and whose sigh was precious; in America one who draws the klipah onto himself by choice is at fault and loses Heaven's help. He adds that the sitra achra invents new forms of 'tichbad ha'avodah', so that the time saved by inventions is filled with new burdens.

title.en: From the drugstore phone to the cell phone

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls when a phone call meant a nickel in a drugstore booth, and how he himself had no phone until a break-in at night. Once everyone has a phone, he says, people are busy with it all day, and now cell phones make them walk around like zombies; he grants a businessman's need and judges a kollel yungerman favorably, but an always-on cell phone without need draws the klipah and takes away the last moment of peace.

title.en: Phones in the beis medrash

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a man who objected to the sign banning cell phones in the beis medrash because of business emergencies, and explains that a ringing phone brings lightness into learning and davening. He brings a writing of the Lubavitcher Rebbe that a seder of learning should be like Shabbos, and reads 'melech l'sadeh ne'evad' as the king who is really a slave to his field.

title.en: Social pressure: kiddushes, sheva brachos, weddings

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the social culture of having to attend every aufruf, bar mitzvah, vort and several kiddushes after davening, and the new custom of sheva brachos every night, bringing a story of the Skverer Rebbe to ask whether everything Rebbes do must be imitated. He recalls the simple delicatessen at his own wedding, says lavish weddings leave people in debt for life, and calls these pressures part of the klipah of 'tichbad ha'avodah'.

title.en: Going out of this Egypt

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls on everyone to leave this Egypt, gaining time to learn, daven and bring joy into the home, and notes that the pressure causes tension and even depression. He asks that each decision to buy something be weighed against this klipah, says one who frees himself is given calm and joy from Heaven, and closes with the season after Chamisha Asar b'Shevat and the parshiyos of the Exodus.

catalogTitle: פרישות מתאוות: בפרט מתאוות דעיקבתא דמשיחא.

oneLiner.en: At a seudas Rosh Chodesh Adar, the Mashgiach teaches that every person needs pleasure, and a Jew should draw it from Torah, tefillah and avodas Hashem rather than chase the new pleasures the world keeps inventing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with two neglected one-line simanim in Shulchan Aruch, melaveh malkah and the seudah of Rosh Chodesh, and explains the Rosh Chodesh meal as a korban-like feast for the diminished moon and a seudah of Moshiach, tied to malchus beis Dovid and to Shaul's anger at Dovid's family feast. Adar has strong mazal, and Jews sit at this seudah even in a time when the sitra achra rules. Building on Dovid's words 'all my wellsprings are in You', he brings a psychologist's rule that a person must have pleasure, and shows from the Yismach Moshe and Rabbi Aharon of Karlin that tzaddikim had it from Torah and tefillah. The danger is drawing in new taavos, new foods and goyish joys. He then praises the miracle that avodas Hashem survives in galus, including in his own beis medrash, and closes with the Yaaros Devash, whose pleasure was standing in tefillah, and a call to begin Adar with simcha.

en: The seudah of Rosh Chodesh is like a korban for the diminished moon, and a seudah of Moshiach bound up with malchus beis Dovid.
Hashem created man so that he must have pleasure; without any enjoyment a person breaks down.
Tzaddikim who tasted nothing in food had the greatest pleasure, from Torah, tefillah and Tehillim.
The bodily pleasures a person was created with are his test, but drawing in new pleasures and new foods distances him from Hashem.
A Jew must not let goyish joys into his home, even a little, as with chametz.
The survival of avodas Hashem in galus is an even greater miracle than the survival of the Jews themselves.
A Jew should take his pleasure from what Hashem provides, Torah, mitzvos and tefillah, and begin Adar with that simcha.

candidateTopics: miracle of jewish survival in galus

title.en: The neglected seudah of Rosh Chodesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes two simanim in Shulchan Aruch, melaveh malkah and the seudah of Rosh Chodesh, that people do not keep, and tells of a Yerushalmi who left his rental income for Rosh Chodesh meals. He explains the meal as a korban for the diminished moon and a seudah of Moshiach, and shows this in Shaul's anger at Dovid's Rosh Chodesh family feast.

title.en: Adar's strong mazal and 'all my wellsprings'

summary.en: The Mashgiach marvels that Jews sit at a Rosh Chodesh seudah while the sitra achra rules, and explains that Adar's mazal is strong, bringing the Gemara that a Jew should push off a case against a gentile to Adar. Adar is a time of ratzon, and he introduces Dovid's words 'all my wellsprings are in You', warning that he will speak sharply and is speaking to himself.

title.en: Man must have pleasure, and tzaddikim had theirs

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a psychologist's rule that a person fed only through a tube will break down, because Hashem made man to need pleasure. He asks how the Yismach Moshe, who once ate soap water as his supper unawares, fits this, and answers that he had the greatest pleasure from Gemara, tefillah and Tehillim, adding a story of Rabbi Aharon of Karlin and a vort of the Kotzker.

title.en: Natural tests versus new taavos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that bodily pleasures are a person's given test, and holding back from sin is itself kedushah, while one can also enjoy learning. But one who seeks out new pleasures, like lying in a newly bought tub, cannot at the same time feel the joy of a blatt Gemara or Shabbos; Hashem can forgive the natural taavos, but drawing in new ones is far away.

title.en: Joy in avodas Hashem and the new foods

summary.en: From the seder's request to rejoice in Hashem's service, the Mashgiach says every yungerman knows moments of great pleasure in avodas Hashem, on Shabbos, Yom Tov, at the Megillah, Akdamus or in the sukkah, despite times of dullness. Running after the world's new foods, a new cake at every kiddush, distances a person from Hashem and from 'all my wellsprings are in You'.

title.en: Pleasure from Torah, not the spider's web

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up that one should enjoy what Hashem provides, not what the sitra achra offers, reading the Mishnah 'one who enjoys words of Torah' as meaning he no longer draws vitality from the world. The new inventions are a web that traps a person like a fly, so one must hold back from new tests; he applies 'do not rejoice, Yisrael, like the nations' and contrasts a Jewish piece of kugel with goyish pleasures.

title.en: Not even a trace, and the miracle of survival

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he painted it in vivid colors, but even a trace of goyish joy must be kept out like chametz; the beis medrash itself filters out those with no connection to avodas Hashem. He then turns to the miracle of Jewish survival in galus, bringing the Yaavetz's count of the vanished empires, and mentions Paras, which never harmed the Jews.

title.en: The greater miracle: avodas Hashem in galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Jewish survival in galus is a greater miracle than Yetzias Mitzrayim, only hidden in nature like the Megillah, and the survival of avodas Hashem greater still, though the Nazi aimed at the Talmud and today's yeshivos hold more students than all prewar ones. He calls his own chevra Emunas Yisroel one of the great miracles and ties it to the seudas Rosh Chodesh, where the moon that died rises again.

title.en: Gan Eden or Gehinnom in the same davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach laments those who do not take advantage of the beis medrash's davening, especially on weekdays, and brings the Gemara that Gan Eden and Gehinnom are one place: the same davening is Gan Eden for one and Gehinnom for another. Other shuls draw people with bagels and lox; theirs serves Nishmas and Shabbos tefillos, and a person should enjoy Hashem's recipe, not foreign foods.

title.en: The Yaaros Devash's pleasure in tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Aharon's saying that he does not trust a bochur until he sees him as a yungerman, and urges continuing. He reads a letter of the Yaaros Devash about his long kavanos in tefillah, for which people laughed at him, and his answer that standing before Hashem in tefillah is his portion. He closes that Rosh Chodesh Adar is a time to begin with the simcha of Torah, mitzvos and tefillah, with a brachah.

catalogTitle: פרקי אבות פרק ששי: “זוכה לדברים הרבה” - תורה היא מועט המחזיק את המרובה. “נקרא רע” - קשר בינו ובין ה'. “אוהב את המקום' אוהב את הבריות.”

oneLiner.en: On the Mishnah in Avos 6:1, the Mashgiach explains that Torah is the small thing that holds the many, that the whole world exists to serve the tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah, and that through Torah he becomes a friend bound to Hashem and a lover of Hashem and of every Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'he merits many things' and explains that the root of everything is a small point that contains the many: Rosh Hashanah for the year, the place of the Mikdash for the world, and above all the Torah, which is our Mikdash. A child and the greatest gedolim learn the same Chumash, yet each sees more. One who learns lishmah becomes part of Torah, and his words too contain much. He then explains that the whole world was created only to serve such a tzaddik, with the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of the collapsing building, Ben Zoma, the nations in Avodah Zarah and a merchant's mashal. From the Maharal on the Torah beginning with a beis he shows that Torah turns curse into blessing, and that with emunah nothing bad exists. Finally he explains 'rei'a' and 'ohev', the union of the tzaddik with Hashem, and why loving a Jew is loving Hashem.

en: The root of every realm is a small point that contains the many, and the root of all roots, of places and of times, is the Torah.
Unlike worldly wisdom, which holds no more than the paper it is written on, the same Chumash and Gemara a small child learns hold what the greatest gedolim see in them.
One who learns Torah lishmah becomes a real part of Torah, so his own words too become 'many things' that contain much.
The whole world, including the nations in exile, exists only to serve the tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah, whether they know it or not.
Torah turns curse into blessing; for one with full emunah everything Hashem does is good, and nothing bad exists for him.
Through Torah the one who learns becomes united with Hashem, so he is called both 'rei'a' and 'ohev', and loving every Jew follows from loving Hashem.

the world created for the tzaddik
union of the tzaddik with Hashem

title.en: Torah: the small that holds the many

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'he merits many things' through the idea that the root of each realm is a small point holding the many: Rosh Hashanah for the year, the Mikdash for the world, Eretz Yisroel, and above all the Torah. He contrasts worldly wisdom, which holds no more than its paper, with the Chumash a child learns and the gedolim see more in.

title.en: Becoming part of Torah; learning as a korban

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who learns lishmah becomes part of Torah, bringing the Gemara of Moshe Rabbeinu and Rabbi Akiva, and shows how one word yields many. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that learning the parsha of korbanos earns the reward of the larger korban, and tells how Rabbi Elchonon Wasserman answered a man who had not seen the reward the Gemara promises for Kiddush.

title.en: The whole world is worthwhile for him

summary.en: On 'the whole world is worthwhile for him' the Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Berachos, the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of a great building that stood only to shelter a tzaddik from rain, and Ben Zoma's blessing on the crowds. Like the limbs of a body, every part of creation serves the tzaddik, even the nations in exile, as a teacher serves a king's son.

title.en: The nations' roads were made for Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Avodah Zarah where the nations will claim they built markets and roads for Yisroel, and explains that in truth every road, invention and telephone exists for the sake of a Jew's learning or mitzvah, though the builders meant only their own needs.

title.en: The merchant's ships: why it is worth it

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how it can be worth creating a world where the wicked outnumber the tzaddikim, and answers with a mashal of a merchant who sends twenty ships knowing nineteen will sink, since one ship's profit covers all. So too the tikkun one tzaddik brings outweighs the loss of many reshaim.

title.en: Torah begins with a beis, above the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal that Torah is above the world: creation starts with a beis while the Aseres HaDibros start with an aleph, and in Tehillim 19 Torah is the eighth passuk after seven about creation. He then brings the Midrash that beis stands for berachah, and explains that where Torah is, even the aleph of curse turns into blessing.

title.en: Ha'azinu, emunah, and nothing is bad

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the parshiyos of Ha'azinu do not end on a good word, and answers that Ha'azinu is the foundation of emunah, and with emunah nothing bad exists. He tells of Reb Zusha, who told the Maggid's visitor that nothing bad had ever happened to him, and explains that at Matan Torah, with 'Anochi', even the bitter is sweetened and turns to good, like the chametz of the Shavuos loaves.

title.en: Rei'a and ohev: union through Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal's distinction that friendship (rei'a) is mutual while love (ohev) can be one-sided, and explains that the one who learns lishmah merits both because Torah, Hashem's own wisdom, binds the upper and lower worlds into one. He brings the Midrash that in the future 'kadosh' will be said before tzaddikim, which will then be understood as Hashem's own honor.

title.en: Shlomo on Hashem's throne; Hashem revealed through the tzaddik

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shlomo HaMelech sat 'on Hashem's throne' because in him people saw Hashem's kingship, and brings the Midrash that one who serves Hashem becomes like Him, as tzaddikim also revived the dead. Hashem is revealed through the tzaddik, so he is a friend bound to Hashem and loved by Hashem and by Yisroel, and he loves Hashem and people.

title.en: Two friends in Rome; loving a Jew is loving Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story brought by a commentator on 'love your fellow as yourself, I am Hashem': two friends in Rome each wanted to be hanged in the other's place, and the king asked to join their friendship. He explains that one loves a Jew because of his G-dly portion, so the two mitzvos of love are one, and that the higher a person rises, the more he is bound to other Jews.

catalogTitle: The War Against עמלק & חמץ

oneLiner.en: On the eve of Rosh Chodesh Nissan, with Jewish soldiers fighting in Iraq, the Mashgiach explains that the days of the Nesi'im and the clearing out of chametz are Klal Yisrael's real war against Yishmael, Amalek and the yetzer hara.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a call from a former talmid, now an army chaplain on his way to Iraq, and urges the bochurim to daven and learn for the Jewish soldiers; learning and davening are the real weapons. He then turns to the minhag of reading the Nesi'im in the first twelve days of Nissan, and explains why a minhag can outweigh a halacha: a practice that all of Klal Yisrael takes on is a kind of prophecy that Hashem puts into their hearts. The Nesi'im of Yisrael stand against the twelve Nesi'im of Yishmael, and Rosh Chodesh Nissan, the new year for kings, is a day of great power. Chametz is the yetzer hara, rooted in Amalek, as the Radbaz answers from the Zohar; Avraham's war against the four kings on Pesach parallels the ways of destroying chametz. He ends with renewal: the whole of Nissan is like Rosh Chodesh, and one must leave atzvus behind and come to Hashem with simcha.

en: The Mashgiach says the bochurim must daven and learn seriously for the Jewish soldiers in Iraq, since learning and davening are the real fighting and a blatt Gemara is a weapon.
A minhag accepted by all of Klal Yisrael outweighs a halacha, because Hashem puts it into the hearts of the people as a kind of collective prophecy.
The twelve Nesi'im who brought the offerings for the dedication of the Mizbe'ach subdue the twelve Nesi'im of Yishmael, so reading the Nesi'im is a weapon against Yishmael.
Each of the first twelve days of Nissan governs one month of the year, and any ten Jews who daven with kavanah on Rosh Chodesh Nissan have a say in the heavenly court.
Chametz is the yetzer hara, which Amalek controls; this is why the Torah is stricter about chametz than about other aveiros.
Avraham Avinu's war on Pesach against the four kings, the four kingdoms of galus, corresponds to destroying chametz through the four elements.
All of Nissan carries the holiness of Rosh Chodesh, a time to renew oneself, and the atzvus that follows an aveirah is worse than the aveirah itself.

title.en: A chaplain's call and the war in Iraq

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a call from a former talmid, now an army chaplain heading to Iraq, who told him there are over a thousand Jewish soldiers there. He urges the bochurim to daven and learn for them, calling a blatt Gemara a 'MOAB' bomb and Amen yehei shmei rabba a Patriot missile.

title.en: The Shivas Yemei HaMilu'im and the Nesi'im

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the seven days of the Milu'im before Rosh Chodesh Nissan and the minhag of reading the Nasi of each day during the first twelve days of Nissan. Unlike Chanukah, where it is a takanah, in Nissan it is only a minhag, and some are lenient about it.

title.en: Why a minhag is greater than a halacha

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a minhag can override a halacha, giving the example of Hallel with a brachah on Rosh Chodesh, which Sefardim say without a brachah. He explains, citing the Kuzari, that a practice all of Klal Yisrael takes on is a prophecy Hashem puts into their hearts, from a higher source than a takanas Chazal.

title.en: Nesi'im against Yishmael; Rosh Chodesh Nissan

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Nesi'im of Yisrael subdue the twelve Nesi'im of Yishmael, so reading them during the battle for Baghdad is a weapon. Rosh Chodesh Nissan is the new year for kings, when the Ba'al Shem Tov secluded himself; any ten Jews davening with kavanah have power above, and each of the twelve days governs a month.

title.en: Chametz is the yetzer hara, rooted in Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach says bein hazmanim is for helping prepare for Pesach and clearing out chametz, which is the yetzer hara controlled by Amalek. He brings the question why chametz is treated more strictly than other aveiros and the Radbaz's answer from the Zohar, then the story of Reb Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev and the women kashering their dishes before Pesach.

title.en: Avraham's Pesach war and the four elements

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that Avraham's war against the four kings is the war against the four kingdoms of galus, and shows from the passuk and Rashi that it took place on Pesach. The four kings correspond to the four elements, and the ways of destroying chametz (burning, wind, water, bitul) use those elements; Avraham defeated them by throwing earth.

title.en: Renewal in Nissan, without atzvus

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shelah that all of Nissan has the holiness of Rosh Chodesh, and calls for teshuvah and renewal as nature renews itself. He warns that the atzvus after an aveirah is worse than the aveirah, notes that Adam was created on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, and closes with a story about davening with simcha because 'we are Your children'.

catalogTitle: פרקי אבות פרק ששי: תורה - מגלה סודות ללומד תורה לשמה' ת"ח משמח המקום והבריות' מלבשתו ענוה' ומרחקתו מן החטא' תורה מביא לומדיה לתיקונם' תורה למעלה מעוה"ז

oneLiner.en: Going through the praises of one who learns Torah lishmah in Avos chapter six, the Mashgiach explains that Torah lifts a person above this world, to the 'eighth' level of yovel, Binah and neder, which frees him from sin and from his troubles.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the mishnah of Torah lishmah phrase by phrase. Learning lishmah uncovers the love of Hashem hidden in every Jew and brings love of Jews; the world is sustained in the merit of tzaddikim; Torah clothes a person in humility. Torah keeps him from sin: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey would not eat untithed food, and the Yeshuos Yaakov sensed a cake was not kosher. It brings him to his purpose and to the tikkun of his soul, so he need not return in another gilgul. From the Maharal on Tehillim 19 he develops that Torah belongs to the 'eighth', above the seven days of nature: Shavuos, the soul, yovel, which Sha'arei Orah identifies with Binah, Yom Kippur, the shofar, milah and neder. With the Ramban on neder and shevuah, the neder against the Canaanite king, and the daily checking of tzitzis, he shows how a Jew connects to that higher world when tefillah alone does not break through.

en: Every Jew has a natural love for Hashem that is only covered over, and learning Torah lishmah uncovers it; love of Jews follows, and is a measure of one's love of Hashem.
Torah keeps its learner from sin to the point that even his possessions, as an extension of his soul, are guarded, as with Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey.
A person was sent into the world on a mission to serve Hashem and rectify his soul; Torah keeps him aware of that purpose so he need not come back in another gilgul.
Torah belongs to the 'eighth', a world above the seven days of creation, which is why it is the eighth verse of Tehillim 19 and why Shavuos, the soul and yovel all share this level.
Yovel, the root of every Jewish soul, guarantees that no Jew is lost: even one sold to idolatry must be redeemed and return to his root.

A neder reaches higher than a shevuah: a shevuah is 'by Hashem' within the seven of this world, while a neder is 'to Hashem', to Binah above it, so a neder, the shofar and tzitzis can bring salvation where tefillah does not reach.

candidateTopics: love of Hashem and love of Jews

title.en: Torah lishmah: loving Hashem and His creatures

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens the mishnah of one who learns Torah lishmah and the passuk that all a man's wealth is nothing against love. He explains that every Jew's love of Hashem is only covered, Torah uncovers it, and love of Jews is the measure of love of Hashem.

title.en: The world is sustained by tzaddikim; humility as a garment

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows from Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and from Adam's task in Gan Eden that the whole world's blessing comes through Jews who learn and serve Hashem, as man is the soul of the world. He then explains that Torah 'clothes' its learner in humility, since true anavah is too lofty to be reached by effort alone.

title.en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey

summary.en: On 'it distances him from sin' the Mashgiach brings the Gemara of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey that would not eat untithed food, and explains with the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person's food and possessions are part of him and come to him by hashgachah pratis to be rectified, so his holiness extends to them.

title.en: The Yeshuos Yaakov's cake; Torah guards its learner

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Yeshuos Yaakov avoided a cake that turned out not to be kosher, and explains that Heaven guards one who learns lishmah. Like the eishes chayil who protects her husband, Torah guards its learner, as Dovid HaMelech said his feet led him to the beis medrash.

title.en: Sent to the world on a mission: 'Ayekah'

summary.en: On 'it brings him close to merit' the Mashgiach explains that a person comes into the world on a shlichus, and tells how the Ba'al HaTanya explained Hashem's question to Adam, 'Where are you?', as a question to every person about his place in the world. Torah keeps a person mindful that he is only a guest here, and shows each one his own path.

title.en: Torah brings the tikkun of the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Elimelech was punished for leaving Eretz Yisrael and answers that his tikkun could have come through Torah. With the Maharal on Tehillim 19 he shows that Torah, the eighth verse, is above nature and 'restores the soul', and with the Bnei Yissaschar that whoever has not fulfilled all the mitzvos must return.

title.en: Sefirah, Shavuos and the eighth world

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls this world a fair where one buys what to take back to the World to Come, and explains that some mitzvos and times draw the 'eighth world' above creation down here. Torah is one of them, which is why Tehillim 119 runs through the alef-beis eight times, and Shavuos, after seven weeks of refining the middos, brings heaven down to earth.

title.en: The soul's root: yovel and Binah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the soul comes from the eighth world, and from the haftarah's 'by the yuval it sends its roots' that yovel means the source. Torah is the root of yovel and of freedom; Sha'arei Orah calls Binah yovel, and in the yovel year each one returns to his field in Eretz Yisrael, his root.

title.en: No Jew is lost: sold to an idol

summary.en: From the passuk of a Jew sold to the 'eiker' of a stranger's family, which Rashi explains as sold to idolatry itself, the Mashgiach teaches that even a soul sold to the Satan is sold only until yovel. Hashem will not let it remain there; idolatry will have to give up every Jewish soul it swallowed, and it must be redeemed.

title.en: Yovel's names: geulah, Kippurim, shofar, neder

summary.en: Following Sha'arei Orah, the Mashgiach explains yovel's names: geulah (the Exodus, mentioned fifty times), Kippurim (Yom Kippur, when Jews live like the World to Come), the shofar that breaks the harsh judgment of Rosh Hashanah, and milah and healing on the eighth. Its last name is neder, which lifts a person above his troubles, as Yaakov vowed in his distress, and Kol Nidrei readies a person to connect to Yom Kippur.

title.en: The Ramban on neder and shevuah; tzitzis

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Ramban in Parshas Matos: a shevuah is 'by Hashem' and a neder 'to Hashem', because shevuah comes from sheva, the seven of this world, while a neder reaches Binah, above it. He adds that tzitzis, the part of the garment that does not warm, reminds a person of what is above nature, and that such things free him from troubles where tefillah does not help.

title.en: The neder against the Canaanite; checking tzitzis

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Parshas Matos, with the laws of nedarim, is read in the Three Weeks, and why Jews made a neder only in the war with the Canaanite king, when tefillah could not help. He then answers why the poskim say to check one's tzitzis every morning: before the battle of davening one connects to the eighth through their eight threads, and tzitzis is tied to geulah, as the Gemara in Berachos shows.

catalogTitle: הספד: על אדמו"ר מסאטמאר זצ"ל

oneLiner.en: Before Rosh Hashanah, the Mashgiach speaks about the Satmar Rav after his passing, explaining that a tzaddik whose Torah is still learned and whose path is still followed has not truly departed, and describing his holiness, prayer, Torah and his battle for a pure belief in Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'Atem nitzavim hayom', Rosh Hashanah as the judgment of every day of the year, and the losses of the year, the last of them the passing of the Satmar Rav. He chooses not to give a hesped but to speak about the tzaddik, since speaking of a tzaddik draws holiness. From the Midrash that 'every illness and every plague not written in the Torah' is the death of tzaddikim, he explains that this curse exists only in the Oral Torah and cannot be reversed, unless the tzaddik's wisdom is not lost. Through Eliyahu, Elisha and a sefer of the Satmar Rav he concludes that learning a tzaddik's Torah keeps him alive. He then describes the Satmar Rav's Torah, kedushas habris, his krias haTorah, Megillah, Ahavah Rabbah, Shabbos and Yom Tov, tzedakah, his last instruction about kohanim, and compares him to Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai and Chizkiyahu in his fight for a pure geulah. He closes with the orphaned generation and the call to hold to the tzaddikim's mesorah.

en: Rosh Hashanah judges every day of the coming year, which is why it is called 'hayom'.
The Mashgiach does not give a hesped but speaks of the tzaddik, because speech draws down what is spoken, and speaking of a tzaddik draws kedushah and taharah.
The death of tzaddikim, a curse hidden in 'every illness not written', is only the loss of the tzaddik's wisdom; where his Torah is learned, he is not truly gone.
The Mashgiach describes the Satmar Rav's holiness, his Torah lishmah, his prayer and the way Shabbos and Yom Tov showed on his face.
Like Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai, the Satmar Rav fought for a pure geulah, and according to the Mashgiach, those who still believe in Moshiach's coming owe it to him.
The generation is left orphaned, but for those who hold to the tzaddikim's mesorah and learn their Torah, the tzaddikim have not passed away.

candidateTopics: learning a tzaddik's Torah after his passing
belief in the coming of Moshiach

title.en: Atem nitzavim and a year of losses

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'Atem nitzavim hayom': Rosh Hashanah judges every day of the year. Had one known in Elul what this year would bring, one would have prayed harder; the gedolim were taken one after another, last of all the Satmar Rav, and he mentions the great mitzvah of a hesped.

title.en: Not a hesped, but speaking of the tzaddik

summary.en: Following those who for certain reasons do not say hespeidim, the Mashgiach will only speak of the tzaddik: speech has the power to draw down, as with hekdesh and terumah, so one speaks only good. He brings the Chasam Sofer on the Gemara 'be warm at my hesped, for I will be standing there': the departed speaks through the speaker.

title.en: Death of tzaddikim, and why Ki Savo says 'arur'

summary.en: Nitzavim comforts after the curses of Ki Savo, and a Midrash reads 'every illness and every plague not written' as the death of tzaddikim. The Mashgiach recalls asking his young cheder pupils why the Torah writes only 'arur' when Rashi says 'baruch' was also said; a child answered that Hashem left the blessing for the Oral Torah, which he supports with the Gemara on Chulda's mercy.

title.en: The one curse the Oral Torah cannot reverse

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar: Rabbi Yossi asked why Ki Savo has no consolation, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai answered, from Eliyahu, that its curses are all blessings and are meant for the nations. The Oral Torah turns the curses around, but the death of tzaddikim is not written at all; it exists only in the Oral Torah, so nothing can reverse it, unless the tzaddikim are not truly gone.

title.en: Eliyahu, Elisha and learning the tzaddik's Torah

summary.en: From Rashi on the passing of Eliyahu, the Mashgiach shows that the bnei haneviim lost their prophecy, while Elisha received a double portion. He brings the Satmar Rav's own sefer: when the tzaddik's Torah is learned and one attaches to him it is not death of tzaddikim; it is only when his wisdom is lost.

title.en: The sweetness of his chiddushei Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges learning the Satmar Rav's sefarim, full of guidance in avodas Hashem and of chiddushim whose sweetness makes one smile, 'sweeter than honey'. He describes his total mastery of Torah and explains with 'pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev' that a chiddush that gladdens the heart is a sign of Torah lishmah.

title.en: Kedushas habris and the power of his words

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Satmar Rav as a tzaddik of earlier generations: great tzaddikim attested to his purity, he did not sleep in a bed except Friday night, and once at three in the morning he was seen learning. In the Shovavim weeks his words on kedushas habris brought thousands to tears, because one can only give others what one has oneself.

title.en: Bereishis, the Aseres HaDibros, the Megillah and Ahavah Rabbah

summary.en: The Mashgiach recounts hearing the Satmar Rav lain 'Bereishis' so that even the walls felt Hashem creating the world, and the crowds, including the elderly Rabbi Yonasan Steif, pushing to hear the Aseres HaDibros. He describes his Megillah reading, brings the story of Rabbi Shalom of Belz reading the Megillah before the Chozeh of Lublin, and his long Ahavah Rabbah, recalling the Ba'al Shem Tov that Moshiach tarries because people do not lengthen it.

title.en: A refined body: cherries, Shabbos fish, a changed face

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the Satmar Rav's body was refined: seen through the blinds eating cherries on a Motzaei Shabbos with kavanos, eating not the fish but the Shabbos at his tish, and arranging the fish in a way Rabbi Yonasan Steif saw as holy names. His face changed so much on Shabbos, Pesach and hakafos that one could have taken him for another person.

title.en: Simchas Yom Tov and the freshness of Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'u'smachtem lifnei Hashem shivas yamim' through the Satmar Rav's long na'anuim with the lulav, which filled the beis medrash with joy and chen, which Rashi ties to Yosef's guarding of the bris. On Chanukah every night was for him like the first, which the Mashgiach connects to his answering the Beis Yosef's question each night.

title.en: Torah from a holy mouth, and tzedakah

summary.en: With 'Torah yevakshu mipihu' the Mashgiach explains that Torah from a holy person is a different Torah; one went to hear the Satmar Rav test his students to sense Torah lishmah, and he adds that children should be given to a melamed who is a yerei shamayim. He then describes how the Satmar Rav taught Williamsburg to give tzedakah beyond its means, even a week's wages at an appeal.

title.en: His last instruction: kohanim, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai

summary.en: At the levayah the Mashgiach heard that one of the Satmar Rav's last instructions was that kohanim not enter the beis medrash. He explains the dispute whether tzaddikim impart tumah, the Yismach Moshe's view, and reads Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai's last words 'clear the vessels because of tumah and prepare a chair for Chizkiyahu' as a ruling that tzaddikim do impart tumah, with Chizkiyahu, master of tumah and taharah, coming to greet him.

title.en: Purity in the camp and the Rambam's Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells from a survivor's article how the Satmar Rav kept clean in the concentration camp and kept his beard. He explains that great tzaddikim sensed he could have led toward Moshiach, as with Chizkiyahu and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai, but the 'biryonim' spoiled it; he reads the Rambam's description of Moshiach as the pure Moshiach the Satmar Rav wanted.

title.en: Belief in Moshiach owed to the Satmar Rav

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that today's belief in the coming of Moshiach is owed to the Satmar Rav, who alone cried out when many called the state the geulah, and he tells of a speech at a Mizrachi convention asking prayers for his health. He compares him to Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai, who asked for Yavneh and was called a traitor yet was the true 'doresh l'Tzion'.

title.en: True lover of Zion, and the Kosel ruling

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the Satmar Rav the true lover of Zion who could tolerate no stain on the geulah. He explains his ruling against going to the Kosel, which was not generally accepted, with the Gemara of Rav Ketina mocking a necromancer so that people would not be drawn after him: the ruling protected even those who go.

title.en: Levi, the last of the Shevatim

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the Satmar Rav a tzaddik of earlier generations and laments the orphaned generation left like a small boat in the sea. He paints the scene of Levi, the last of the Shevatim, telling the Jews in Egypt about Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, and their despair at his passing; the Midrash on 'Yosef and all his brothers died' answers that the One Above did not die, and he adds that Shimshon's might outlived him.

title.en: Following the footsteps of the flock

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Pesikta that the tzaddikim of the churban are greater than those of the binyan, relative to what is expected of their generation. With 'tz'i lach b'ikvei hatzon' he says that whoever holds to the tzaddikim's mesorah and learns their Torah keeps them alive; he ends with hashgachah, emunah until Moshiach, and blessings for the new year.

catalogTitle: שמיטה: שנה של התפשטות ירושלים על כל א"י וכל יהודי נעשה ללוי (שייכות ליו"ט סוכות)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yerushalayim is always in a state of shemitah, that in the seventh year its holiness spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael and every Jew becomes like a Levi, and that the sukkah brings a Jew into Yerushalayim wherever he is.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens on Sukkos, whose center is Shemini Atzeres, when the Torah reading speaks of shemitah. Shemitah teaches that a Jew is a stranger: his field and his money are not his own. Using olam, shanah and nefesh, he explains that Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of place as shemitah is the Shabbos of time: Yerushalayim was never divided among the tribes, its houses are not rented, nothing is planted there, and it belongs to Hashem. In the seventh year Yerushalayim spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael and every Jew becomes like the tribe of Levi. Shemitah is therefore a tosefes, an addition to Yerushalayim, which is why Rabbi Akiva learns tosefes from it. Finally the sukkah is Yerushalayim and the Holy of Holies; entering it is like fleeing to Eretz Yisrael, which reopens a verdict. He closes with the 122 days from Elul to Zos Chanukah, a call not to waste them, and words on the geulah of a lowly generation.

en: Shemitah teaches that a Jew is a stranger in this world: his field and even his money are not his own, and he must trust Hashem.
Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of place just as shemitah is the Shabbos of time, so in Yerushalayim it is always shemitah.
In the seventh year Yerushalayim spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael, and every Jew becomes like the tribe of Levi, without a field of his own.
Shemitah is not something new but a continuation and tosefes of Yerushalayim, and so it is the root of every tosefes, including tosefes Shabbos.
The sukkah is Yerushalayim and the Holy of Holies, so a Jew who enters it is like one who flees to Eretz Yisrael, where his verdict is reopened.
The 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu match the 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah, and these days must not be wasted.

the days of judgment until Zos Chanukah

title.en: Shemini Atzeres and the lesson of shemitah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens on Sukkos and says that all the Yamim Tovim revolve around Shemini Atzeres, when the Torah reading speaks of shemitah. He explains that shemitah teaches a Jew that he is a stranger whose field and money are not his own, and that he must trust Hashem.

title.en: Yerushalayim, the Shabbos of place

summary.en: Using olam, shanah and nefesh from Sefer Yetzirah, the Mashgiach shows that the Holy of Holies, Yom Kippur and the Kohen Gadol meet on one day, and that Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of place as shemitah is the Shabbos of time. In Yerushalayim it is always shemitah, and in the seventh year it spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Yerushalayim belongs to no one

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares shemitah and Shabbos, which are 'for Hashem', with Yerushalayim, which has nothing of its own: nothing is planted there, it was not divided among the tribes, and its houses are not rented. Like a kallah who receives everything, the land is Hashem's; Yerushalayim is a place of Torah, and in the seventh year its state flows over all of Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Yaakov, the tribes and Levi

summary.en: The Mashgiach traces Klal Yisrael from the individual Avos to Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, from whom the twelve tribes branch out. Yaakov is Shabbos and the tribes are the weekday Roshei Chodesh; Eretz Yisrael was divided among the tribes, but Yerushalayim belongs to the trunk, and Levi, who has no portion, is shemitah. In shemitah every Jew becomes like a Levi, a taste of the World to Come.

title.en: Eating Shabbos, eating shemitah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the eating of Shabbos carries great holiness and tells of chassidim whose Shabbos fish and challah held Shabbos itself. He then shows that in shemitah one eats 'yashan', the old, like the 'atika' of Shabbos, and that eating shemitah fruits brings yiras Shamayim and puts a Jew into Yerushalayim even outside it.

title.en: Shemitah as the root of tosefes

summary.en: The Mashgiach says shemitah brings nothing new; it is Yerushalayim flowing over, a tosefes like tosefes Shabbos. He brings Rabbi Akiva's teaching in Rosh Hashanah that tosefes is learned from shemitah, asks why the passuk begins with Shabbos and ends with shemitah, and answers that shemitah is itself the tosefes of Yerushalayim and so the root of every tosefes.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva, the man of additions

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from his rebbe, Reb Gedalya Schorr, that every mitzvah has a point that spreads to all mitzvos, as parah adumah is the root of every chok; shemitah is the root of tosefes. Rabbi Akiva, who descended from converts, who are an addition to Klal Yisrael, expounded the crowns on the letters and taught tosefes from shemitah.

title.en: Shemitah for Jews outside the land

summary.en: Shemitah, like Shabbos, is a kallah and carries a scent of the geulah, when Eretz Yisrael will spread over the whole world. The Mashgiach explains that its holiness cannot rest on the land of chutz la'aretz, which belongs to the nations, but it does rest on the Jew there and on his money, as Reb Tzadok shows from the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair.

title.en: The sukkah as Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one sentenced who flees to Eretz Yisrael has his verdict reopened, and the seforim that the sukkah holds the air of Eretz Yisrael. He brings the Radomsker's question on 'in the place Hashem will choose', and the Sar Shalom of Belz: Sukkos is Yaakov, to whom Yerushalayim came in chutz la'aretz, so a Jew in a sukkah anywhere is in Yerushalayim.

title.en: Fleeing into the sukkah reopens the verdict

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that the sukkah joins the names Havayah and Adnus, like the keruvim spreading their wings over the kapores, so sitting in the sukkah is sitting in the Holy of Holies. A Jew who flees into the sukkah after Yom Kippur is like one who flees to Eretz Yisrael, where Hashem Himself judges, and there is only mercy.

title.en: This year and the sukkah's protection

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that this year, 5768, Sukkos and shemitah meet, a double holiness of Yerushalayim, and that it is a year spoken of as fit for geulah. He explains that the segulah of the sukkah is protection, tells how the Belzer Rav stood at the Shabbos candles for hours during a war saying 'ufros aleinu sukkas shelomecha', and urges keeping the sukkah with all its hiddurim.

title.en: The 122 days and Parshas Ki Savo

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that the time of judgment extends to Hoshana Rabbah and, from the Arizal, to Zos Chanukah, and tells how the Maggid of Mezritch tested a new ba'al korei on how the parshiyos relate to the week. The pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu hint at these days, 122 in all, and Ki Savo is a mussar on the 122 days of the past year that were wasted.

title.en: The world needs a reckoning

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the whole world, America as well as Eretz Yisrael, needs a reckoning. He tells how, when he was in Eretz Yisrael some years earlier, he answered someone afraid of the intifada that he was afraid to go to America, and soon after his return came the Twin Towers, as a Gemara about a plague in Eretz Yisrael implies. Now Hashem has given the sukkah and new 122 days, and one must not wait.

title.en: Geulah through the lowly generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the geulah will not come through the greatness of the great generations but through the lowliness of the last one, like the aravah, the lowest of the minim. As Simchas Torah joins the end of the Torah to Bereishis, the lowly generation will be joined to Moshiach, and he closes with blessings for a good year.

catalogTitle: A Month of תחיית המתים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Nisan as the month of revival, in which Hashem renews His plan for a perfect world again and again, and shows how matzah, as a key of chesed from a world above time and space, opens a Jew to that renewal.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens on Chaf-Hei Adar, recalling the Gemara's dispute whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nisan, and notes that Hashem's 'regret' is language for our understanding, since everything was in His plan. He then describes Nisan as a series of attempts at a perfect world: Adam HaRishon, Avraham Avinu the 'spring neshama' and Yetzias Mitzrayim spoiled by the Egel, the Mishkan spoiled by Nadav and Avihu, and a fourth Nisan of Moshiach that will succeed. From the Mishkan built and taken apart for seven days he draws the message never to despair after a fall. Nisan is a month of chesed, harnessed chesed, which he illustrates through the right hand, the lunar calendar balanced by the solar year, and Shabbos in the middle. Matzah is the key that opens the doors of chesed; its gematria of three times Mah shows it comes from a world above time and space, unlike bread. He closes with Pesach as the beginning, the bris of the Jew with Hashem, and a story about davening for a kosher Pesach.

en: Nisan is the month of renewal in which Hashem 'tries again' for a perfect world: with Adam HaRishon, with Yetzias Mitzrayim, with the Mishkan, and finally with Moshiach.
Avraham Avinu is the 'spring neshama' of Klal Yisroel, and the main events of his life took place on Pesach.
Nisan is a month of chesed, the midah of Avraham, but Jewish chesed is harnessed and balanced by din.
Matzah is the key that opens the doors of chesed and brachah on Pesach; Targum renders matzah as 'patira', opening.
Matzah comes from a world above time and space, which is why it may not be given time to rise, while bread depends on both.
Pesach is the beginning, the bris that ties a Jew to Hashem, so eating chametz brings kares, the opposite of that bond.

title.en: Creation day and Hashem's first plan

summary.en: On Chaf-Hei Adar the Mashgiach recalls the Gemara's dispute whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nisan, and explains that when the Torah speaks of Hashem 'regretting', it speaks in our terms, since even Adam's sin was in His plan. He describes the world Hashem intended with Adam HaRishon on Rosh Chodesh Nisan: a Gan Eden without death, spoiled by the sin of the Eitz HaDaas.

title.en: Avraham Avinu, the spring neshama

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every person has his time, and Avraham Avinu's time is Nisan, the spring. He paints spring as a revival from the shrouds of winter, brings Shir Hashirim's call to wake up, and lists the events of Avraham's life that took place on Pesach.

title.en: The second and third Nisan

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Hashem's second attempt, localized to one nation descended from Avraham and brought out of Mitzrayim in Nisan, which the Egel spoiled. The third attempt, localized to the Mishkan, was spoiled by Nadav and Avihu, and Rashi on 'Mishkan haEidus' hints that the two Batei Mikdash would be destroyed.

title.en: The fourth Nisan and never despairing

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the promised fourth Nisan with the third Beis HaMikdash, when death will end, as the Rambam describes at the end of Hilchos Melachim. He connects this to the Haftarah of the dry bones read on Pesach, and draws from the Mishkan built and taken apart for seven days that a person who falls must get up and try again.

title.en: Nisan, the month of chesed

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nisan is a month of chesed because it is Avraham Avinu's month, and that creation in Nisan reflects building the world with chesed rather than din. Jews always raise chesed over din: washing the right hand first, putting on the right shoe first but tying the left, binding tefillin on the left, and writing from the right.

title.en: Harnessed chesed: moon, sun and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Esav, who writes from the left and follows the sun of din, with Yishmael, the refuse of Avraham's chesed, whose unbridled chesed turns to immorality. Jews count by the moon of chesed but harness it to the solar year through the leap year, while the Arabs' months drift through the seasons; likewise Shabbos stands in the middle between Friday and Sunday.

title.en: Matzah, the key that opens

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nisan goes straight, like the aleph-beis, and opens with chesed: maos chittim and 'whoever is hungry, come and eat'. Matzah, which Targum calls 'patira', is the key that opens the doors of chesed; on Pesach night the storehouses of tal open, as the Targum Yonasan says about Yitzchak's brachos, and tal in gematria joins the Name of Hashem and brings down the tal of techiyas hameisim.

title.en: Matzah, Mah and the night of questions

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pesach comes from a world beyond understanding, the world of 'Mah', and that matzah equals three times Mah (45) while bread equals three times the Name Havaya (26). That is why the Haggadah begins with questions, and why Pesach is renewal, when people buy new clothing and take out vessels unused for a year.

title.en: Matzah above time and space

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that this world is bound by time and space, as shown by how witnesses are examined on when and where, while bread needs both to rise. Matzah is given no time and takes no space, because it belongs to a higher world, and on Pesach a Jew is to rise above them. He ends with the two pieces of matzah at the Seder, the Afikoman pointing to the future redemption.

title.en: Pesach as the beginning and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that although Shavuos and Sukkos are higher, Pesach is the beginning, when a Jew ties himself to Hashem, so chametz carries kares, the opposite of that bond, and an arel may not eat the korban Pesach. He brings the Radbaz's question why chametz is treated more strictly than any other aveirah.

title.en: The tzaddik's kernel of wheat

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story he heard from the Klausenberger Rebbe about a tzaddik who prepared a perfectly chametz-free Pesach and found a kernel of wheat in his soup. Through a she'eilas chalom he learned that he had not davened for a kosher Pesach, and that a bird had dropped the kernel through the chimney. The Mashgiach closes with a brachah for a kosher Pesach in Yerushalayim.

catalogTitle: מאכלות אסורות: דרוש בענין: גודל הפגם של מאכלות האסורות ותיקון למי שנפגם בזה (שייכות לסוכות ושמ"ע ופרשת ראה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why forbidden food does such deep damage, dulling the heart and cutting a Jew's felt bond with Hashem, and shows from the order of parshas Re'eh that the repair is holy eating and wholehearted teshuvah, which is why the end of Re'eh is read on Shemini Atzeres.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Sukkos as a return to Gan Eden after Yom Kippur's atonement for Adam's sin, and Shemini Atzeres as the peak of all the Yamim Tovim, which needs a teshuvah greater than Yom Kippur. He then lays out parshas Re'eh: it opens with eating kodshim in Yerushalayim, turns to the meisis and the forbidden animals, and returns to aser te'aser. Eating is the gravest act because food becomes part of the person; forbidden food dulls the heart and breaks the felt bond with Hashem. He illustrates that bond with the halacha of a bas Levi, the Lechovitcher's cry and Baal Peor, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that even one damaged through his parents can purify himself. A long discussion of Rosh Chodesh, melacha as Adam's curse and women's sensitivity follows. He ends that holy eating, the Shabbos table and wholehearted teshuvah on Shemini Atzeres repair the damage.

en: Eating is graver than other acts because the food becomes part of the person, and forbidden food dulls the heart so that one no longer feels kedushah or has desire to learn and daven.
Parshas Re'eh opens with holy eating in Yerushalayim, moves to the meisis and the forbidden animals, and returns to aser te'aser; the middle is the damage and the end is the repair.
A Jew who truly feels his bond with Hashem cannot be talked away by a meisis; one who falls has lost that feeling, and the Torah traces it to forbidden food.
Even someone damaged through no fault of his own, through what his parents fed him, has no excuse: by strengthening himself with all his strength in avodas Hashem he can purify himself completely.
The repair of the damage is holy eating in a holy place: the Shabbos table, eating together with Jews, the sukkah, netilas yadayim and bentching with kavanah.
Shemini Atzeres, a day of love after the awe of the Yamim Noraim, is a time of teshuvah with the whole heart, and that is why the closing parsha of Re'eh is read on it.
